speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEMBERSHIP OF THE SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON A RENEWED CANADA-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Before we proceed to Government Orders, I wish to share with hon. members the Chair's ruling on the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead earlier this week.
Wednesday, September 25, 1991, the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead raised a question of privilege concerning the membership of the Special Joint Committee on a Renewed Canada. He alleged that when the committee started sitting, it did so unlawfully because, first of all, the report of the House Management Committee listing the membership of the Special Joint Committee was filed with the Clerk of the House after the hour of adjournment on Tuesday, September 24, and an order adopted by the House on June 19, 1991, did not prescribe this procedure for a day when the House was sitting.
Second, he objected to the fact that the House Management Committee's report listed 22 names of members, while letting the Whip of the New Democratic Party select two members from a list of four names to fill two of the three seats to which the party was entitled on the Special Joint Committee.
The hon. members for Saint-Leonard, Cape Breton-East Richmond, Calgary North and Saint-Denis, and the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council intervened to clarify certain points for the Chair, and I appreciate their contribution.
Before responding to the specific points raised by the hon. member, I must inform him that the question he raised is not a question of privilege. However, there is
certainly some basis for raising a point of order, and the Chair's response will be along those lines.
Regarding the first point raised by the hon. member, I wish to point out that the wording of the special Order, adopted by the House on June 19,1991, and published in the Votes and Proceedings of that day at page 226, does not refer to adjournments of the House but simply to those times when the House is not sitting, which in the Chair's opinion may include extended periods of adjournment such as the summer recess, shorter periods of adjournment such as from one sitting day to the next, or the period comprised by the weekend.
Consequently, the Chair rules that the report filed by the House Management Committee with the Clerk at 7.28 p.m. on Tuesday, March 24, was filed in accordance with the Order of the House of June 19, 1991 and therefore does not present a problem.
I also wish to point out to the hon. member that said report was published in the Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, September 26 and was available on the Table of the House on September 25.
Let us consider the second point raised by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead.

The report of the Standing Committee on House Management lists the initial membership of the special committee and goes on to note how the NDP Whip will fill two of the three places allotted to the party. It is important to note that under the terms of the special order, the Whip of each party is given full control of the membership for that party and the power to substitute at will.
Do the terms of the standing committee report reach back into the special order and put constraints on the NDP Whip by stating that in filling two of the three places allotted to the NDP, their Whip is limited to choosing from the pool of the four NDP members named in the report? The Chair's reading of the committee's report cannot conclude otherwise. And yet, does this not impose a restriction on one of the parties that

September 27, 1991
Speaker's Ruling
was never envisioned in the terms of the order of June 19, 1991?
Under ordinary circumstances the standing committee report would have been presented to the House and could have been scrutinized by the House before a motion for concurrence was entertained. There would have been ample opportunity for the House to seek clarification of questions raised by the unusual form of the report. However, the terms of the order of June 19 last have, in effect, denied the House and the Chair such an opportunity by deeming the report concurred in.
We are now faced with scrutinizing the terms of the report after the fact; indeed, after the special committee has held its organization meeting, elected its officers and begun its hearings. In departing from the strict terms of the order of June 19, 1991, which instructed that a 20-member committee be struck, and in deviating from the traditional form of reports for striking committee memberships, the Standing Committee on House Management has placed the Chair in a quandary. The procedural authorities warn against the consequences of such action. In Bourinot Parliamentary Procedure fourth edition, at pages 469 to 470, it states:
It is a clear principle of parliamentary law that a committee is bound by, and is not at liberty to depart from, the order of reference. This principle is essential to the regular despatch of business; for, if it were admitted that what the House entertained, in one instance, and referred to a committee, was so far controllable by that committee, that it was at liberty to disobey the order of reference, all business would be at an end; and, as often as circumstances would afford a pretence, the proceedings of the House would be involved in confusion.
The interventions of hon. members Wednesday made clear that the report has, indeed, sown widespread confusion about the membership of this special committee. The difficulty lies in the designations member No. 19 and member No. 20, and in the explanatory note narrowing the terms of the order of June 19, 1991. This cannot be allowed to stand.

The Order of the House of June 19, at page 226 of the Votes and Proceedings, provides in the second paragraph that the House Management Committee will simply "designate" 20 members of this House as members of
the Special Joint Committee. There is no reference to additional members or members designated by numbers marked with an asterisk, in connection with a list of substitutes.
In Canadian parliamentary practice, a striking committee has a very narrow mandate.
Unless the House specifically authorizes them to do so, such committees may only report names of members who are to sit on parliamentary committees.
By failing to observe the Order of the House of June 19, the House Management Committee went beyond its mandate. At first, the committee appointed only 18 members; subsequently, it proposed a substitution procedure for two numbered seats set aside for the NDP.
The Chair finds the second part of the House Management Committee's report clearly inadmissible, and in this respect, the objection raised by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead is well founded.
That being said, should the Chair therefore reject out of hand the report of the House Management Committee, with all the serious consequences this might entail? I think it would not make sense to reject all the work done by the House Management Committee and the Special Joint Committee. The three Whips were acting in good faith in their concerned efforts to respond to a request by the New Democratic Party.
I therefore see no satisfactory reason for starting the selection process over again and thus forcing the Special Joint Committee to interrupt its work. Consequently, the Chair rules that the 18 members designated as members of the Committee were formally appointed by the House pursuant to the report of the House Management Committee and in accordance with the Order made on June 19; the Chair also rules that the remaining part of the House Management Committee's report is null and void. Finally, the Chair asks the Striking Committee to file a supplementary report, in addition to the report filed on September 24, designating two more members of the New Democratic Party, and when this report is tabled in the House or filed with the Clerk, pursuant to Order of June 19, said supplementary report shall also be deemed to have been adopted pursuant to Order of June 19, 1991.
September 27, 1991

In concluding, the House will understand that this ruling is an unusual one on the part of the Chair, but it is not unprecedented. On February 14, 1944, and April 23, 1975, the Chair intervened in matters concerning committee reports. Those instances were not entirely identical to the question before us today, but the intent of today's ruling reflects the intent of the rulings made by my predecessors, who in similar circumstances also refused to categorically bring the business of the House to a halt.
I wish to thank hon. members for their patience.

As I was saying, the Canada Assistance Program is very important. It was started by the Liberals in 1966. Even the Nielsen report, which was commissioned by the Conservative government as to finding ways that we could streamline government, make it less expensive and more efficient, said that CAP or the Canada Assistance Program was a very good program. It lauded the way that the program had made for more harmonious relations between provinces and Ottawa, although it did concern itself with the cost, particularly the open-ended portion of the Canada Assistance Program.
Because the Nielsen report concerned itself with the cost and the open-endedness, this fifty-fifty cost sharing program, the government many years later, about actually a year ago, gave clear signs that it intended to cap CAP. Once again I say that the program gives constitutional responsibility for income redistribution including social assistance programs to Canadians anywhere in Canada. In every province one would have an equal chance of obtaining an equal amount of money.
This concerned a great deal the Conservative side of this House mainly because of the expense. Of course it is a fifty-fifty cost sharing deal. Whenever the provinces had increased costs, they can rely upon the federal government to pay 50 per cent of those increased costs. That was the seed of discord or discontent on the government side because the federal government was seeing the provinces increasing their costs and it did not have much of a say except to pay the increased costs itself.
So a bill came down. It was Bill C-69 and it imposed a two-year freeze on the CAP for British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario. It is interesting that Bill C-69 considered British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario as rich provinces. If we take a look at Ontario right now with the unemployment, the deficit, the recession, and the problems that free trade caused in Ontario and for a lot of other people, we see that Ontario is far from being a rich province.
British Columbia too.

British Columbia, my hon. member tells me as well. What we have here is a definition of provinces as being rich when they are not. With Bill C-69 and imposing a two-year freeze I believe we have the
government trying, to the best of its ability perhaps, to cut expenses and at the same time doing it on the backs of people who are least able to afford these cuts.
Bill C-69 was challenged. It went to the Supreme Court of Canada, after winning in the lower courts, the courts of first instance. The provinces challenged the bill saying: "The government made an agreement with us that it was going to pay for these programs". When a government makes a political agreement, and with this government where political agreements we thought were sacred, we find that that is not the case. If you shake hands-
A sacred trust.

"A sacred trust", the member from the government side says. We have heard that before.
The Supreme Court decision essentially said no, that Parliament is supreme, that Parliament can shake hands with you at one moment and then stab you in the back at the next, and that when Parliament is in session, if you accept the supremacy of Parliament, no one's purse or life is safe.
We saw that very clearly with Bill C-69. Now we are looking at, as a result of the Supreme Court making it very clear that Parliament has this power, the government coming back again with Bill C-32, which extends the freeze for three more years.
Our party is very much concerned about this. We have to look behind the freeze and see who does this affect mostly. We have to look at the people who are mostly concerned with the Canadian Assistance Program. I will just give a very quick rundown of who these people are: abused and neglected children in need of protection obviously, mentally and physically disabled persons, one parent families, seniors, the unemployed and the working poor, battered women, families and individuals in crisis.
Because of the capping of CAP there has been a movement on the part of a number of provinces. I can tell you in particular about the movement in Ontario and by our party here in Ottawa. We wanted to put into the Constitution a social contract, provisions whereby the people I have just named would be protected. There would not be a constitutional right for the government to make an agreement and then go back on its word.

People ask: "How will this social contract immediately affect myself or Canadians?" It would not allow the government to do what it did under Bill C-69 and what it is trying to continue to do under Bill C-32. It is extremely important when we talk about a social contract that our fellow Canadians understand that what we are trying to do partially is to repair the abuse-and I would say the abuse of process, even, although it was legitimate according to the Supreme Court decision-that we saw the government do in its initial legislation, Bill C-69, and is continuing to do in this legislation, Bill C-32.
Therefore it is obvious that our party is against this piece of legislation. We were against the practice. We did not think it was fair in these constitutional times, I can tell you.

Madam Speaker, I do not know the number of times I have risen to speak about the port of Halifax, either in direct relationship to the At and East subsidy or on other matters relating to the crisis situation affecting the port of Halifax today.
The At and East subsidy maintained fixed rail costs for moving grain and flour to eastern Canadian ports, notably the port of Halifax and the port of Saint John, New Brunswick. It was designed to make these eastern Canadian ports competitive with ports on the eastern seaboard of the United States and other Canadian ports. It was a simple theory and one that worked.

September 27, 1991
Government Orders
In July 1989 the At and East subsidy ended without, I might add, the benefit of legislation. On July 15, 1989 the subsidy was cut and the fallout began in the port of Halifax and in the port of Saint John. We have waited for the government either to see the error of its ways or at least bring the bill through the House. Finally, here we are two years and two months later, two years and two months without this subsidy, and now we have finally reached third reading of this bill. It is not something that will go unnoticed by the people of Halifax and the people of Saint John.
What has been the effect on these two ports of the cancellation of this subsidy? We all know what the effect was on Saint John, New Brunswick. The grain elevator there is closed. The jobs are gone. The port has taken a crippling blow. Elsie Wayne, the well known and articulate mayor of Saint John, has made her plea and it has landed on deaf ears in this government. Saint John has taken a serious, serious wound.
In Halifax the grain elevator is down to one-quarter of its normal capacity. The same can be said for the flour mill in the port of Halifax. The number of jobs lost is a serious blow to the economy of Halifax and the life of the port, which is the lifeblood of the city and to some degree of the province and the region.
In 1988, the last full year of the At and East subsidy, 337,914 tonnes of grains and 182,957 tonnes of flour came into the port of Halifax under the At and East subsidy. According to Captain Claude Bell of the Halifax Port Corporation roughly one stevedore is employed for every 1,000 tonnes of grain and flour exported.
It means that in that area alone we are looking at a loss of approximately 500 jobs in a city with a population of approximately 100,000. This loss is not inconsiderable. This loss is something that can and will create major hardship in a city that for years has prided itself on its self-sufficiency, particularly because of its port.
The At and East subsidy has been in effect since the early 1960s. As I said before, this was to allow the eastern ports of Saint John and Halifax to compete adequately with the superports on the east coast of the United States, New York and Baltimore in particular.
Since the cancellation of At and East-to add insult to injury, to pour salt in the wounds of Haligonians and Dartmouthians and Nova Scotians and New Brunswickers-among other things Canadian Pacific Rail has, with the able financial assistance of this government, purchased the D&H railroad. The D&H railroad out of the eastern U.S. ports is a direct and serious competitor with CN rail on the Halifax to Montreal run. Are there subsidies any more for CN rail? No. At and East is dead. Even without legislation it has been dead for two years, two months and two weeks.
At and East is dead but D&H is thriving. D&H is going along just fine, thank you very much, with the able assistance of the Government of Canada. There are jobs in Maryland and New York State. Those ports are getting along just fine. There are jobs on the D&H railroad.
What is happening in Halifax, what is happening in Nova Scotia? Five hundred jobs lost at the port, more jobs lost from the rail and so on and so on; a litany of disaster that is epic in its proportions. But that is all right. Let the free market forces bear. Things are good in Baltimore and New York. Halifax will just have to learn to get along without the assistance of the national government.
At and East has some other ramifications for the people of Nova Scotia as well. I am going to leave the full description of these problems for my colleagues who know more about the agricultural industry than I do.
I want to talk about one thing. In Nova Scotia this year we had a wonderful summer of weather as far as tourism was concerned. We had hot sunny days and beautiful blue skies. However, in the month of July we had one-quarter our normal rainfall. Consequently, for farmers in the province of Nova Scotia the hay crop is less than half its normal annual output. That is going to make things very tough for livestock farmers in the province of Nova Scotia.
What was the other benefit from At and East to the people of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island? It was a fairly good and reasonably priced source of feed grain. That is gone. The hay crop is less than half its normal output. The livestock producers in the province of Nova Scotia, and in the maritimes generally, are going to suffer as a result of that. I know that my colleagues who know a great deal more about agriculture would agree with me that this is going to be a very, very difficult time for livestock producers in Nova Scotia.
September 27, 1991

The province of Nova Scotia is a small province. When one sector is hit the spin-off, the bouncing ball effect, the ripple effect hits everyone in the province. That is why Haligonians are as concerned about the Sydney steel plant as residents of industrial Cape Breton. That is why the people of South West Nova are as concerned about the port of Halifax as Haligonians. That is why all Nova Scotians know that the problems of the farmers throughout our rural areas are problems for all of us.
We are small. The population of the province is at most 800,000. In the metropolitan area represented by the member for Dartmouth and myself-and I believe there is another member, but I cannot remember who it is at the moment-250,000 of those people live. However, they are concerned about the whole province and the economic future and stability of that province.
At and East has been effectively dead for two years, two months and two weeks. Today, the government finally puts the bill through for the last time. The people of Nova Scotia and the people of Halifax-Dartmouth will remember. They will remember well who caused their once mighty port to suffer and decline. Nova Scotians have long memories.

Madam Speaker, as you mentioned, earlier, it is a Friday morning. The Chamber usually has some of its better speeches on Fridays because the members know we have to ensure that the government has learned its lesson for the weekend until we return on Monday. I hope that in the few moments I have, I will instil a little discipline on the other side.
I have spoken to this bill that is before us a number of times, as have other members on this side of the House. It is a regressive piece of legislation that the government bungled when it first tried introduce it.
The member for Halifax indicated that the At and East subsidy, which was an absolutely essential part of our grain transportation system and infrastructure in Canada, has been dead for awhile. It has been over two years now.
Government Orders
The government introduced a bill, and before the bill ever passed it decided that it was going to do away with the subsidy.
I spoke, and I think this is the third time, in debate on this so I am not going to speak specifically about the impact on the agricultural sector in Atlantic Canada, particularly Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, of the removal of the subsidy. Suffice it to say that this is one of those examples of the government selectively deciding to punish Atlantic Canada for being the eastern part of the country or maybe because it saw good sense in the last election and elected mostly Liberals.
Unfortunately, the people of Atlantic Canada, who knew better than to try and re-elect this government because they knew what in the name of goodness was going to happen to the country, elected Liberals. We will have to wait a little longer to rectify the damage that has been done by this government's policies, particularly in Atlantic Canada.
I want to talk a little bit about what has happened to the port of Halifax. The At and East program, a subsidy for the movement of feed grains to east coast ports, is gone. I have said in previous speeches that I am certainly not one of those people who gets up and says: "Well then you should do away with any freight rate assistance in western Canada or you should go up the St. Lawrence Seaway and do away with any infrastructural subsidy that takes place". There is free ice-breaking, free aids for navigation and things like that on the St. Lawrence Seaway.
Surely to goodness there is something called fairness. If the government is going to treat us one way, then everybody else should receive the same treatment. If it is going to treat the west one way it should treat the east the same way. This government does the old divide and conquer. At the port of Halifax, the loss of the At and East program was just one in a number of crippling body blows inflicted by this government.
My hon. colleague from Halifax spoke very succinctly about the problems in the port of Halifax that had been caused by the loss of the At and East subsidy. She talked about the 500 jobs that have disappeared in an area of only 100,000 people.

September 27, 1991
Government Orders
But more than that is happening in the port of Halifax. Just to give you an idea about what the At and East started, I want to let you know what has happened in Halifax in the last 12 months. The port of Halifax is one of the most efficient ports in North America. It is not one of these places where one says: "Well, there is a lot of fat to cut, so you should cut the fat and you will be more competitive," It is extremely competitive and that is recognized in the shipping industry around the world.
There is a problem because the government's transportation policies have caused the port of Halifax not just to lose $20 million or $30 million, but if one adds the At and East subsidy loss to the loss of traffic in the last 12 months, we are looking at nearly $60 million worth of traffic. We are looking at 500 jobs lost with the reduction or the elimination of At and East, and we are looking at at least another 400 jobs that have been lost in the last number of months.
This government has been asked repeatedly in the House of Commons to address the problems facing the port of Halifax, to stop its assault and battery on the port of Halifax and its business, and it has consistently refused to do so.
Another little body blow was delivered just in the last little while. The government has decided to change some of the regulations dealing with meat inspection on frozen meat that enters Canada. Why in the name of goodness would it do that? Was it because it did not think it was efficient? No. It was because Canadian Pacific rail lobbied the government effectively to change the regulations.
ment care? Does the government care that a change in one regulation might lose that traffic to the port of Halifax and might put it through the ports in Philadelphia or New York? It does not care at all. It did not even consult with the industry, it changed the regulation.
The At and East was the beginning of a large crack that this government instituted in the competitiveness of the port of Halifax. I do not think it is about to end. I asked in this House for the Minister of Transport to order the National Transportation Agency, the NTA, to hold an inquiry because we have heard from people in the industry that things like the loss of the At and East, things like a less than competitive schedule by Canadian National, things like perhaps a too high fee per tonne shipped by Canadian National between the port of Halifax and the inland ports in Montreal, or even perhaps the fact that the St. Lawrence Seaway is subsidized.
They tell us in Halifax when we deal with trains shipping things from the port of Halifax to Montreal or Toronto that it has to be full cost recovery. After all, that is why we lost At and East. That is why it cannot look at freight rates or try to lower the rates that CN charges because there has to be cost recovery.
Madam Speaker, do you know what? We lost business and 400 jobs in the port of Halifax when Hapag-Lloyd left and took $24 million in traffic with them. Do you know where it went? Fifty per cent of it went to New York, 50 per cent went up the St. Lawrence Seaway to Montreal.
The regulations usually work like this. When frozen meat products come into Canada, through a port usually, it is inspected at the port. However, now that Canadian Pacific has acquired the D&H line through the United States and is actively undercutting ports like the port of Halifax, what has it done? It has said: "Look, federal government, we have to get more traffic moving towards central Canadian markets through our ports in the United States because we've got a rail line there. If you just change your regulation that any frozen meat product that is coming into Canada via a U.S. port will not be stopped at the border and will only be inspected when it reaches the warehouse, we'll be able to steal some business from ports like Halifax".
Approximately 50,000 tonnes of frozen meat product was imported through the port of Halifax last year alone from Australia and New Zealand. What does the govern-
All we are asking for in the east is not that other places get pummelled and kicked and battered like Atlantic Canada, but we demand fair treatment for the Atlantic coast transportation infrastructure and most importantly for the ports on the Atlantic coast.
This is not the last time, Madam Speaker, that you are going to hear myself and other members from the Atlantic speaking. Because, if we lose our transportation infrastructure, if our ports lose their competitiveness because of negligence or because of design by this government, through things like the loss of the At and East, we will not be able to compete. We are in a period of constitutional renewal again and we are talking about trying to ensure equality in this country. Yet every single time that the government decides to come in and save a dollar here or a dollar there, it seems to hit the Atlantic harder than anywhere else.
September 27, 1991

There was a document released yesterday by this government. It talked a great deal about the need for an economic union. I fully support that. I think nearly every Canadian would support the idea of unrestricted movement of goods, traffic and people in this country. But, my goodness, how can one legitimately have an economic union in this country when the government, by every action it has taken in the transportation sector in Atlantic Canada, has removed or lessened our ability to trade and compete internally?
If the port of Halifax is weakened, if we lose a container terminal, if we lose a flour mill, if we lose a grain elevator, it means we cannot compete. If it allows Canadian National to keep its rates high so nobody will bother shipping through our ports but will go down and ship through the United States, very soon after CN will say: "You know, our traffic has decreased because of our rates and our service, therefore we are going to apply for rail line abandonment". We have heard this story before. We have been at this movie. We did not like it then and we certainly do not like it now.
In conclusion, this bill has been before this place so often I might have spoken on it 10 times. If I could get away with it, I would speak on it 20 times because this is a bill that shows callousness and the absolute lack of good judgment. This is the type of bill that goes a long way to destroying unity in this country, because the country is not going to stay together if people do not believe it is in their economic interest. When you see a government single out any region of this country for particularly brutal treatment by the way it legislates, if you think that does one thing for national unity then I should have a chat with you because I certainly do not think it does.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to rise today and participate in the debate on the At and East freight rates. As eloquent as the statements by the members from the Atlantic provinces may have been, this is not merely an Atlantic problem. I would like to explain why that is so.
In previous stages of this debate, a debate which has been going on for a long time, western members of the New Democratic Party have stood solidly with people from Atlantic Canada to fight this particular manoeuvre, and I think people are aware of that.
The reason we have fought this is because the principles at stake here are very important, and there are several of them. First of all, what we are looking at here is another case of the government dismantling the infrastructure that holds this country together, particularly the transportation infrastructure. This country was originally built on a transportation infrastructure. The national dream of John A. Macdonald and his successors was clearly based on tying this country together economically with a transportation infrastructure.
Our agricultural economy was based on that. It was early recognized that our major grain producing regions in this country, in other words the prairie basin, were far removed from any kind of tidewater, far removed from ports where grain could move into export markets. This is in contrast to all our major grain competitors in the world. In Australia virtually all the grain is grown within 200 miles of the coast. The same is true in Argentina. United States has major waterways. The Mississippi river system which empties its heartlands provides for cheap water based transportation out of its heartlands.

Government Orders
Western Canada and the prairies were the only grain producing regions in the world, virtually, that did not have a big enough internal market to absorb its production, and that was far from tidewater.
The infrastructure that was put in place was a very important part of the fabric of this country. It was particularly an integral part of the agricultural industry as it developed in this country.
What have we seen? We have seen this whole infrastructure come under increasing attack by a change in philosophy that says that infrastructure is not important, that it is not the government's job to ensure that the larger picture is looked after, that it is merely the government's job to make sure that whatever entrepreneurial organization or corporation, be it a railway, grain company or whatever, can make an extra dime on $1 million here or there.
This government and the government before it had abandoned the idea that it is the job of the federal government in this country to hold the infrastructure together. The erosion obviously started with the whole attack on the Crow rate, which I remember so well as being launched by the former Minister of Transportation, Jean-Luc Pepin.
Although we still have a western transportation act that includes some elements of that old Crow rate structure, certainly the major part is gone. Year after year it is being eroded and made less and less effective.
Another critical element of that whole debate is this At and East question. What At and East did was two things. First, it allowed western grain to get to the maritimes at a competitive rate so that the maritime agricultural industry had access to that grain. Second, it allowed for an alternate set of ports to be used in times when they were needed. Particularly that was important because these are ports that are open 12 months a year and not frozen in, in the winter, as the Great Lakes ports are.
We do have ports on the west coast that are open all year round, but we do not have any way to get to the Atlantic Ocean 12 months a year without going to the maritime ports. At and East gave us the capacity to do that.
What have we seen? We saw what I think is one of the most shameful legislative processes that I have seen take place since I became elected in 1988. Surely it is incumbent on the government to treat its own legislation and its own legislative processes with some respect, but it did not do that in this case.
It must have felt that somehow or other the maritime voice would not be heard here, that there were so few farmers in maritime Canada that their voice would not be heard or that the 500 workers who are about to be laid off or who have lost their jobs did not matter. I do not know what the thinking of the government was. I have trouble reading its mind.
What I do know was that on July 19, 1989 the government unilaterally, and probably illegally, cut off the At and East payments. It made them inoperative and it has been operating on that basis ever since.
Here we are over two years later still without legislative authority to consummate what the government had done by fiat. That is a totally unacceptable way of going about things from a legislative point of view, especially on a question that is as important to the national infrastructure as this one.
I would urge government members to reconsider what they have done here, not only in terms of At and East but to make sure first of all that the whole process does not happen again.
I think that if this government has any moral guts and moral convictions it should compensate the people for the losses that they have incurred over the last two years while the At and East rates have been illegally gone.
A further backdrop to this whole situation is the crisis that is facing agriculture in general in this country. Surely this is the wrong time to start pulling apart our agriculture infrastructure piece by piece by piece. We are seeing it happen with rail line abandonment in western Canada. We have seen off-loading of federal cost shared programs like crop insurance on to the provinces which can ill afford them. This is creating a patchwork of programs across the country.
That is the opposite direction from which we would like to be going. A very real cash flow crisis is endangering probably one-third to one-half of Canadian farm families and maritime farm families are no exception.
September 27, 1991

It is making it impossible for livestock producers and for people that depend on the flour milling industry in the maritimes even to plan in the short run, let alone the long run.
It is one more hammer blow to the economic well-being of farmers, not only in maritime Canada, but right across the country. If those maritime markets are lost as a result of the At and East going, it means that western Canadian farmers have one less opportunity to sell their grain within their own market.
I recognize the time is getting short, Madam Speaker. What we need is an agriculture industry that can serve our farming community from coast to coast to coast, that can ensure that we have an infrastructure which can ensure security of food for Canadian families right across this country, and not chip away our security of food supply the way this government is doing.

What the minister is telling Canadians is he is prepared to make them the victims on the battleground of his dispute with his own employees.
Shame.

The public is suffering because this minister and this government are too stubborn to do the right and fair thing and try to get a solution.
I ask the minister one more time to do as we have recommended, to respect the collective bargaining process, which is the law of this land, and appoint a mediator, who is neither friend of the government nor friend of the union, who can bring some fairness, some stability and some sanity to this mess. Will the minister do that or not? If not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the IVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have already indicated to the hon. member that there is an ongoing process. We did not break off negotiations. We made new offers and I expect them to be considered.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
On May 27 in this House I asked the minister to instruct the National Transportation Agency to hold a full inquiry into the competitiveness of the port of Halifax. Instead of an inquiry, we hear now that the minister is considering a new tax on all vessels plying Canadian waters, a new tax which will further reduce the competitiveness of the port of Halifax.
My question is this: Since the minister has said that he is reconsidering this new tax, will he also reconsider my request of May 17 and order the National Transportation
September 27, 1991

Agency to hold a full inquiry into the competitiveness of the port of Halifax?

Madam Speaker, we have been working with the people in the port of Halifax, with the shippers and with the carriers to do what we can to enhance the port of Halifax.
I think the hon. member should take into consideration the fact that the port of Halifax at the current time is certainly in a condition where the tonnage going through the port of Halifax is down.
We should also remember that the port of Halifax right now is well above where it was five years ago. Historically it has been a victim of the cyclical change as far as transportation and shipping are concerned. We know it is in a downturn right now and we are working with the port to attempt to help in whatever way we can to increase tonnage through the port.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is on the same issue, but it is for the Minister of Agriculture.
The government has bowed to pressure from Canadian Pacific Railway and has changed its regulation with respect to the inspection of refrigerated meat products entering Canada. The result of this change is that it will be easier for imported meat products to enter the Canadian market through U.S. ports, not Canadian ports.
Given the fact that the port of Halifax sees over 50,000 metric tons of refrigerated meat products go through its port every year, I want to ask the minister if he will immediately rescind these new regulations which are going to be crippling and perhaps be the death-knell on the competitiveness of the port of Halifax.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we all know that from time to time we have problems with the borders in some specific cases, as the hon. member is mentioning. However, we should know that Canada is a net exporter as well in this sector and we must be very careful about import-export regulation at the borders.
What we want is to be more competitive and get more products out of the borders as well, to improve our capacity to export. We have the capacity to look after
Oral Questions
those borders and those regulations. I can assure the hon. member that we are going to look after these problems and get back to him on the specifics.

Madam Speaker, I want to return to the Constitution and ask the Deputy Prime Minister, whoever that may be, a question.
Under the proposed amendment to section 121 of the Constitution, which will now read to include, if passed, the free flow of not only goods but also of services, people and capital, I would like to ask the minister, for example: What would happen if this section is part of the Constitution to a Crown corporation like Sask Energy in Saskatchewan that Grant Devine tried but failed to privatize two years ago? If this provision were in effect, would it require, for example, Sask Energy in that case to be privatized, forcing it to live by the same legal and financial and tax regimes as the private sector and private energy corporations? Would that be the case under the free flow of capital under section 121?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the intent of article 121 is very clear but, as was raised by the hon. Leader of the Opposition earlier on about the les offices de commercialisation, it is written later on that certain institutions like those in particular which are targeted would be protected under a national interest.
Bill C-21 indicates that we should strive to remove all the obstacles, most of them, but we make provision for regional development, for regional disparity and for other interventions which might be judged to be of national interest.
In any case, it is only when the proper legislation is drafted that we can see how this will apply. I am not in a position at this time to pass judgment on the interpretation of a piece of law which has not even been written yet.

Madam Speaker, I think that is the very case in point. Here is the government minister saying he cannot pass judgment on law, and yet they are proposing the constitutional amendment. Sask Energy is not a marketing board. What guarantee is there that it be declared in the national

Oral Questions
interests? Those are the questions I ask. They are very important, Madam Speaker.
In addition to that real question, I would like to ask the following of the minister. In The Toronto Star this morning the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs is saying that once a provincial government opts in to a certain provision under the new amendment to section 91 of the economic union, a subsequent government cannot opt out. Thus that subsequent government is committed to the guidelines of the previous government. In the words of the minister, and I quote: "You are caught, you are bound in that situation", which theoretically means that the Ontario government might have been prevented from taking its most recent direction in its budget a few months ago.
The Minister of Finance said the opposite. My question is: Which minister has the proper interpretation- the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs who said there is a prohibition or the Minister of Finance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say in terms of the aspects being raised by the hon. member about the budget making process or the macroeconomic approach that what we have proposed is basically something which should be obvious to all Canadians. We have 11 governments operating in this country. Surely they would not want to be at cross purposes. In my view it is very clear that provincial government are sovereign governments. In the end, if they can get into a deal, the same method should allow them to get out of it.
In my view the problem raised by the hon. member does not exist. What we want is to create a mechanism whereby governments can sit together, look at the situation together, try to reach a consensus, and then hopefully act accordingly for the good of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Last Saturday I had the honour to be in Armenia as Canada's official observer during their historic referendum for independence. The Armenian citizens voted overwhelmingly, 99.31 per cent, for independence to rid themselves of the oppressive yolk of communism which lasted over seven decades. The atmosphere was euphoric on Saturday, but now the new government must face the harsh realities toward building a free-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member does have a question.
Madam Speaker, my question is: Will Canada work closely with the Armenian government to provide all possible technical aid and assistance as it builds for the future?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I want to thank the hon. member for acting as my personal representative at the referendum on independence which did indeed produce excellent results for Armenia.
We will be ready to stand by and assist in Armenia. I would point out that during the earthquake a couple of years ago in that region, Canada was one of the first and major donors and, that in London this summer at the G-7, the Prime Minister committed $25 million to technical assistance within the republics of the Soviet Union. That funding too will be available to the Armenians.
We have a task force actively engaged in assessing Canada's expertise and how it can be matched. I am sure that Canadians of Armenian descent as well will want to be involved directly in assisting their country.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Transport.
September 27, 1991

CN is selling its rail line from Truro to Sydney, Nova Scotia. Tenders are being called today. This line is vital to the economy of eastern Nova Scotia, including to Stora Forest Industries on which more than 2,000 jobs directly depend.
Why has the minister allowed CN to sell this vital rail line in Nova Scotia?

Madam Speaker, CN has made a proposal under a formula that is possible within this country. The one caveat that is in there is that the bid received will not be entertained if it does not maintain the same level of service that is currently there on that particular line.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I remind the minister of section 99 of the Financial Administration Act which authorizes the Governor in Council to issue directives to Crown corporations.
Will the minister direct CN today to stop its privatization of the Truro to Sydney line? I also remind the minister of the Route Canada application in which the government allowed CN to privatize Route Canada and a few years later it went bankrupt.
Madam Speaker, until the tenders are placed, until the offers are received and until we see what the entire situation is on that line, no decision will be made.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
This weekend marks the first anniversary of the United Nations World Summit for Children. Its main goal was to encourage governments to sign and ratify the Convention on the Rights of the Child. As we know, Canada has yet to sign and ratify this convention.
My question to the acting Prime Minister is what steps does the government still have to take before honouring this agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Secretary of State of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think this government and the Prime Minister have made it very clear that we have a longstanding commitment to this particular process and
Oral Questions
things are advancing as they should. We maintain that commitment. The Prime Minister has made it time and time again.
I would just like to reiterate to my hon. colleague that our position has not changed.

Madam Speaker, that is the most frustrating answer I have ever received in this House. We know that money to help the needy is scarce at all levels of government, and especially since this government has put a cap on CAP, which is where the money is going to have to come from.
Given this strait-jacket that the government has put on the provinces, I really would like to ask the minister whether this convention and the summit have merely been an exercise in public relations by the Prime Minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, absolutely not. I have been in New York for most of this week at the United Nations and I raised the issue of the children's summit a year ago in my speech. I also was discussing with colleagues in other countries the over-all and co-ordinated response that we are expecting.
Canada will be responding veiy shortly. We have worked very actively on our response. I am sure the hon. member will be pleased when she sees it, and she will see it very soon.

Madam Speaker, the bankruptcy statistics, which were released today, shows signs that the recession is not over and that recovery is still stalled. Business bankruptcies are up 7 per cent since July, and over all bankruptcies are up 17 per cent from last year.
I would like to ask this government what it is doing to change its economic policies given that unemployment is rising, given that the manufacturing sector output is falling, and given now that business bankruptcies are increasing?
Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and
Privatization)): Mr. Speaker, the rate of bankruptcies in this country is totally unacceptable. We do not take enjoyment in seeing either personal or business bankruptcies.

Oral Questions
One thing I can say, however, is that the rate of bankruptcies, the trend, is down not up and that is a positive sign. We believe with the drop in interest rates, which again dropped yesterday some nine bases points, that that trend has continued over a period of time. We believe that will help businesses naturally recover and recovery in this country.
We, of course, still firmly believe, and we have great support in that, in getting inflation down and interest rates down. Keeping them both down is going to be the best thing we can do in this country for business recovery. We are working toward that end.

Madam Speaker, the government claims in fact that lower inflation is the path to recovery and yet the Bank of Canada has just reported that 41 per cent of present inflation has come from the GST and other taxes.
Why is the government pushing up inflation with these taxes at the same time that it claims to be seeking lower inflation? Surely there is a major contradiction here that is hurting people right across this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is right. One thing he fails to point out though is that the government predicted that inflation would increase 1.25 per cent because of the goods and services tax. That is exactly what happened.
The opposition said it would go up 7 per cent, as I remember.
The other major cause of the increase in inflation due to government policy is the increase in cigarette tax. That is the other major reason.
Does the hon. member oppose that tax?

Madam Speaker, my question is for the acting Minister of Finance.
This week, Inter-City Products, a Canadian company, closed one of its American plants and moved jobs to Canada. Last week, Colgate-Palmolive, an American company, closed one of its Canadian plants and moved jobs to the United States.
Would the minister not agree that Canadian owners are more likely to preserve Canadian jobs? If he does, will the government encourage more Canadian ownership by increasing rather than decreasing the dividend tax credit?
. Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and
Privatization)): Madam Speaker, the best way to keep companies in Canada is to ensure that our economic policy, our trade policy and our tax policy are all conducive to international competitiveness. That is what it is all about.
That is what the free trade agreement is all about and that is what the removal of the manufacturers' sales tax which penalized our Canadian producers over their competitors off-shore is all about.
We believe that our corporate tax rate is in line with our competitors, and we adjusted our tax in tax reform in 1987 to that effect.
I read with interest about the 300 jobs that are heading to Brantford. They are closing down a plant in the United States and moving the jobs to Canada.
I visited IBM just recently. It is opening a new plant in Brockville, and it is enlarging its operation in London, all because of the free trade agreement. There is adjustment going on, but there is a lot of good news for Canada in this.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. Yesterday, Donohue Matane Inc. announced it was shutting down indefinitely, laying off 400 people.
Some analysts days that the paper industry cannot compete with the Canadian dollar at 88 cents.
Here is my question to the minister: will the minister review his monetary policy to give a break to a region where the unemployment rate exceeds 25 per cent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will remind the member for Saint-Leonard who just talked about the exchange rate how difficult it is to control the value of the Canadian dollar and correct this idea
September 27, 1991

members opposite seem to have that the government could bring it down artificially at the touch of a button.
Foreign borrowing by the provinces for the first six months of this year totals some $10 billion, which is more than for all of last year. Such loans naturally translate into dollars, creating a huge demand for Canadian currency. So the price goes up. The value of our currency is set by the demand on the market, not by some government decision.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Madam Speaker, maybe I should remind the minister that, just last week, at the 1991 economic rendez-vous in Quebec, the economic stakeholders passed a resolution urging the federal government to act and review its monetary policy to boost, so to speak, Quebec's economy. My question is quite simple. He asked the new minister responsible for Quebec economic development to- the Minister of National Health and Welfare had made a flashy announcement in Matane to save this area with over 25 per cent unemployment. Where is he today? What does he intend to do for these 400 new unemployed men and women in Matane?

Madam Speaker, let me point out to my hon. friend that there are a lot of other factors involved in the decision to curtail production at the Matane mill.
The fact of the matter is that demand has very seriously declined by 10 per cent this year alone. Prices have fallen by 22 per cent this year for this kind of product.
It is tragic of course that a new mill like this, as well equipped as it is in technology, should not have overcome its initial start-up period and break its way into the market.
As I have said, the mill is well equipped with the very best in technology both in the environmental and technical sense. It bodes well for the future. I hope that the shut-down is not for too long a period.

Madam Speaker, in the port of Halifax, the At and East grain subsidy is dead.
Oral Questions
Government contribution to the new double stacking program between Halifax and Montreal is strictly provincial. A new tax is being planned and federal government policy makes it easier to import meat products through American ports into Canada. Yet the Prime Minister said last week that he has concrete proposals.
I ask the Minister of Transport: What are these concrete proposals? For a change, what is the good news for the port of Halifax?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's concern about her particular area of the country and that indeed is why we are all in this House, to work to make this country grow and make it prosper.
As I mentioned earlier, the port of Halifax does have some problems right now. It is caught by a problem with tonnage on the high seas being reduced. Therefore it is no longer going in. The container traffic certainly is down at the port.
It is, however, still higher than it has been in the past. There are projections that it will improve again in the future. In the mean time, we are working with the port. As the hon. member knows, the province has worked. The federal government has worked with port officials to see what can be done.
It is something we must all work together on, along with the member for Halifax. One of the things that she should keep in mind also is that when it comes to port competitiveness, the municipality also plays a part in this. She may know that the municipal taxes paid by the port of Halifax are higher than what it they are in other North American ports, such as New York and Montreal. We all must work together to make the port work more effectively.

Madam Speaker, the question was: What is the federal government going to do? The question has been: What is the federal government going to do? Pretty words and nice phrases will do nothing for the port of Halifax whose business is down from last year, which the minister knows well.
If the minister cannot tell us what the federal government plans to do, and it appears that she cannot, maybe she can tell us why Ports Canada refuses to release its report on the competitiveness of ports like Halifax.

September 27, 1991
Oral Questions
What is the government hiding? What is the bad news?
Madam Speaker, nothing is being hidden. Ports Canada will release that report when it has the report finished and is in a position to-
It's finished.

-and all of the necessary background work is done to release it, it will release it.
The member must also remember that we have to look after all ports in this country, not just the port of Halifax. We are concerned about it.
Oh, oh.
Good job in St. John's.

We are concerned about it.
The hon. member is calling out about St. John's. She might want to talk to her colleague from Thunder Bay-Nipigon about the port of Thunder Bay and how it has benefited by what has been done.
It will sell well in Halifax.

I know it will sell well in the port of Halifax, Madam Speaker, because this member is representing her riding. There are other ridings in this country also that have to be represented when it comes to ports. We are working on the port of Halifax and we will continue to work.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Com-ox-Alberni.

Madam Speaker, last May the government promised to cut Canada's illiteracy rate in half by the year 2000. According to the government's own figures, 4.5 million Canadians are basically illiterate or marginally literate. This means the government will have to come up with funds to provide literacy training for 2.25 million Canadians over the next nine years. Yet there is no new funding in the minister's budget and the minister continues to fund only short-term pilot projects.
My question is for whomever is sitting in for the minister today, or for the Minister of Finance. This is a promise in the last throne speech of this government. How can the government expect to deal with Canada's literacy problems, which are costing this country $10 billion annually unless there is sufficient money in the minister's budget to provide long-term funds to support literacy programs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as the hon. member has correctly indicated, it was referred to in the throne speech, like many other initiatives which are part of the government's global agenda. With respect particularly to prosperity, we all are aware that we have serious problems in this country, one of them being illiteracy, the other one being the drop-out rate in high schools. The government is putting into place the appropriate programs to deal with those problems in co-operation with the provinces which have specific jurisdictions with respect to education.

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
Pilot projects funded by the Minister of Multicultural-ism and Citizenship have a proven record of success in improving literacy. Yet these projects lose their funding after a year or two because of the government department's short-term funding policy.
An example is the Write Place in Parksville, British Columbia, which, although very successful, had its funding cut and was forced to close its doors three weeks ago.
My question to the minister is: Why does this funding program punish success? When is he going to address illiteracy problems seriously by providing ongoing funding for successful literacy programs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board.
A few moments ago the President of the Treasury Board said that agricultural marketing boards would be protected under the national interest clause of the constitutional proposal.
Why then, two days after the constitutional proposal, did the government table the economic union document which qualifies agricultural marketing boards as undesirable trade impediments? Is the government in favour of or against marketing boards? Canadians want to know.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the document on the economic union we list all kinds of organizations or rules preventing full mobility in Canada. Of course, marketing boards are on that list. However, marketing boards serve other purposes also, such as the external market as was well explained by my colleague this morning.
In some instances the national interest would prevail. In this particular instance it is our intention to make it prevail.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the document on the Canadian economic union clearly mentions agricultural supply marketing boards as an internal barrier that it would not be desirable to maintain.
Why does the minister consider our marketing boards to be "detrimental"? Is he for or against marketing boards for our farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)

Point of Order POINT OF ORDER

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:

He read an excerpt in which institutions or obstacles to free movement are mentioned. Obviously, a board that regulates and controls is by definition an obstacle. Some obstacles are desirable. On page 22 of the document on economic union, it says precisely, under "Managing the Internal Market", that the government proposes to adopt laws, programs, practices, but "the amendment -allows for exceptions for reasons of national interest".
I tell him that this is an exception in the national interest. It is on the lower right-hand side of page 22.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I thank the hon. minister, but when making a correction, one should not get into debate. Does the Hon. Leader of the Opposition wish to speak?

In a document, the government says that it wants to maintain marketing boards; in another, it says that it wants to do away with them. Madam Speaker, I ask that Notice of Motion No. 33, standing in my name on the Order Paper under Private Members' Business, be withdrawn.
It relates to amending the Hazardous Products Act for children's sleepwear. There are many times that we criticize the government for not doing what we wish it to do. Madam Speaker, I would like at this time to address the April 1989 budgetary decision of this government that terminated the At and East export grain and flour subsidy. This decision, which was actually implemented in July 1989 reflects the callous disregard that this government has repeatedly
shown toward the aspirations of the people of Canada, particularly the people of Atlantic Canada.
Over two years after the actual implementation of its decision, this government is still seeking the approval of Parliament for its action. Yes, it is seeking over two years of retroactive approval. What a display of contempt for Parliament.
The removal of this subsidy was supposedly made in an effort to reduce government spending and reduce the deficit. No one quarrels with the desire to reduce the deficit, but a little research and two years of experience shows that the removal of this subsidy has had the opposite effect and actually increased the deficit as well as increased unemployment and aggravated other social problems.
In September 1989 the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission submitted a study showing that the net savings in removal of this subsidy would be minimal and that a small, one-time expenditure in the upgrading of the Saint John terminal to enable the off-loading of ships, would have allowed this subsidy to impact positively on the well-being of the economy of the Atlantic area.
Rather than study this document, and have the courtesy to respond to the suggestions contained therein, this government did not even have the courtesy of giving a response to the people of Atlantic Canada.
It would appear that the much touted policy of consultation with the people before a decision is made does not extend to the Atlantic provinces. The closure of CFB Summerside is another example of this.
I would like to take a few minutes at this time to review briefly some of the contents of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission submission. I hope this will remind this government of the Atlantic provinces' desire and need to keep open the terminals at Halifax and Saint John in order to serve the needs of the people in this region and provide jobs.
This study showed that in 1988, the last year that the subsidy was in place, the cost to the Government of Canada was slightly over $32 million. The study also showed that the economic loss of this decision would be approximately $27.5 million, for a net savings of only $4.5 million. The same study showed that upgrading the Saint John terminal by providing a marine receiving facility, so that ships could be unloaded, would reduce the cost of the subsidy by $22 million. This would then change the
September 27, 1991

subsidy from being a cost of $4.5 million to a gain to the economy of $17.5 million if the subsidy was retained.
These figures illustrate that the decision to remove the subsidy was made on the false assumption that there would be a drop in the cost to the Canadian economy when in fact the study showed the opposite effect would occur.
There were other recommendations made that would ensure that the grain elevators at Halifax and Saint John would be able to continue as viable operations and that the export of grain and flour would continue to move through the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
These recommendations included permit plan C feed grain to come to Halifax and Saint John by water; eliminate the countervail duty on U.S. com- I believe this has been done-provide facilities in Saint John to receive grain by water; use the port of Halifax to export flour; allow feed grain to be imported from foreign countries.
When this issue was debated over two years ago, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission said, and I quote:
The termination of the At and East rate structure will have serious economic consequences for the Maritime ports as well as for other activities that depend on the movement of export grain and flour through the ports. These activities include grain elevators, port employment and railway employment. There are also negative implications in relation to flour milling and the movement of domestic feed grains in the Atlantic Region. The importance of maintaining the Halifax grain elevator as a viable operation is of critical economic importance to the entire Atlantic region.
The Saint John grain elevator serves only the export market. However, the rail traffic provided by the movement of export grain over that portion of the rail line from Montreal to Saint John was an important contribution to the viability of that line.
The shipment of export flour through the Port of Halifax contributed significantly to employment at the port.
The At and East export grain and flour subsidy program had important implications for several domestic industries in the Atlantic region, including local livestock producers, flour milling and the railways.
Government Orders
With the cancelling of this program, the continued viability of the grain elevators at Halifax and Saint John is in jeopardy.
Let us now look at what has happened in the two years since the decision to terminate the At and East.
The Saint John elevator has closed with the accompanying job loss. A study of what will make it viable indicates that if this government insists on continuing its present policies, it will never reopen.
Two hundred and fifty tonnes of export grain are required, mainly because the market for feed grain is limited. Without some form of government action, this is an unrealistic expectation.
In Halifax, we now export only 60,000 tonnes of grain. Feed grain demand cannot make up the shortfall. The port needs 400,000 tonnes to make a profit and ensure long term viability. Without some form of government action, this will not happen.
We have already seen substantial job loss at the port of Halifax. The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission in an extensive study this year has concluded, and I quote:
Under current operating circumstances, if the government takes no
action to assist them, the long term viability of grain elevators in
Atlantic Canada is in doubt.
To achieve financial viability requires an increase in export grain for Atlantic elevators. If this does not happen, Saint John will stay closed and Halifax will close.
The loss of this economic activity in the two ports involved will have a terrible impact.
But we must keep in mind what will happen in the agricultural sector. Cost of feed grain is predicted to rise by $10 a tonne. That would make our livestock and poultry industry non-competitive and these industries would die. The warning signs are already there. Only a government as blind and insensitive as this one could ignore these signs.
Atlantic Canada has already been the victim of this government's policies in many areas, the fishery, transportation, small craft harbours, the post office, and the list goes on.

Government Orders
Surely Atlantic agriculture deserves a better fate than that which will surely befall it if the AT and East subsidy is not restored.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I would liJce to rise once again to speak on this legislation. It is a piece of legislation which comes at a time when the transportation infrastructure of Atlantic Canada is so much in peril and under attack. At a time when this government, as announced this week, has proposed major plans to create an economic union and a common market across Canada, the At and East subsidy and the legislation which in effect kills this subsidy without any reasonable form of replacement fly in the face of the laudable objective of creating a viable economic union across Canada.
If in Atlantic Canada we do not have an adequate and competitive transportation infrastructure, which has been part of the reason for being part of this country since Confederation, how can we realistically expect to participate in a viable economic union? Those are the fundamentals of this debate today.
This comes virtually two years after the At and East subsidy was cancelled without even recourse to Parliament. In fact, the previous legislation, Bill C-26, which was in effect in the last Parliament, was enacted after the subsidy had been removed and after the consequences of the subsidy, namely the closure of the Saint John terminal and the downsizing of the Halifax terminal, had already taken effect.
This raises the procedural point related to this legislation, that is the arrogance with which the government has treated this particular matter in initially introducing the legislation after the fact. On top of that, to add insult to injury, it reintroduced it in this Parliament without going through the proper legislative steps which are expected after a government begins a new Parliament with a Speech from the Throne.
The abuse of Parliament and the arrogance by which this legislation was introduced are additional insults to the people of Atlantic Canada.
I do not want to confine my remarks at this time to the procedural matter because the substance of this legislation is also very important. In fact, the At and East subsidy was a vital way of lowering the price of agricultural products produced in Atlantic Canada by enabling grain to move across the country to the farmers of
Atlantic Canada. Therefore, the loss of a subsidy without an adequate replacement places the farmers of Atlantic Canada in additional jeopardy, not to mention the millers in Halifax.
What is also surprising about this whole affair is the fact that the government had an option. The government had an alternative to cancelling this subsidy. In fact, it even commissioned a study which provided the government with a more efficient and viable way of assisting the movement of grain in eastern Canada. This would mean that those people and industries so vitally dependent on this service would not have to go without. They would be able to continue to receive the benefits that the At and East subsidy, perhaps not as efficiently as it might have and perhaps more costly than it might have, provided to the farmers and the millers of Atlantic Canada.
Instead the government has chosen to cancel the subsidy, to eliminate this program, and then come to Parliament a long time after the fact for approval.
This is a further insult to the people of Atlantic Canada. It is an insult because they are losing their vital infrastructure and do not have a sense that they have a say about it. When they offer their opinion, when they agree to participate-as the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission did in working on this study and in providing advice through the committee on transport on how to modernize, update, and re-orient the subsidy programs available to eastern Canada-the federal government has chosen to ignore their advice. It says: "We are pressing on in the way we planned to, thank you very much, but we do not want to listen. We have our minds made up".
It is this kind of disregard for the views of Atlantic Canadians and the associations which represent them which has been a hallmark and a trademark of this government. It is in evidence with this particular piece of legislation.
We on this side of the House want to demonstrate by our opposition to this bill the fact that in Atlantic Canada we are concerned about transportation. We are concerned about being able to play on an equal playing field. We are not willing to accept, lying down, the transportation infrastructure as represented by this piece of legislation.
